newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Tasman Energy, Marlborough Electric weigh merger.
newsitem.headline: Tasman Energy, Marlborough Electric weigh merger.

text.p: NELSON, July 2 - Tasman Energy and Marlborough Electric will decide whether to go ahead with merger plans in the next few weeks, the New Zealand Press Association reported on Wednesday.
Tasman Energy chief executive Bill Luff said the two companies' boards were expected to make recommendations to their respective consumer power trusts by the end of the month.
It would then be up to the trusts to decide whether the merger should proceed, after they had consulted the public, he said.
The merger proposal was floated last year, with the idea being that each company would have a 50 percent share of the new merged company.
However, it was then discovered that the advice on which the 50:50 split was based was flawed.
The two companies could not agree on what their share of the new company should be, so employed independent advisers to investigate their relative values.
Those advisers have now come up with preliminary valuations, under which Tasman would own 57 percent of the new merged company and Marlborough 43 percent.
Luff said the valuations were still being fine-tuned, so the ownership ratio could change by one or two percent. But the basic weighting in favour of Tasman would stay the same.
He said the Tasman board was satisfied with the 57:43 ratio, given the fact that Tasman had a bigger customer base than Marlborough.
Each company's valuation had been based on its projected future cash flow, he said.
Marlborough Electric Power Trust chairman John Cudon said the trust was "not happy" with the 57:43 split because it did not put enough value on Marlborough's assets.
However, the trust was waiting to get the final facts and figures before it made a decision, he said.
"It doesn't mean the merger won't go ahead," he said.
The trust supported the merger in principle because it would result in cost savings, he said.

Tasman Electric Power Trust chairman Peter Malone said his trust had also agreed in principle that a merger would benefit consumers because it would put the two companies in a better competitive position.
